New Middle Cambrian and Middle Ordovician palaeomagnetic data from

13 Abstract N
14 A
15 Whether Siberia was a coherent tectonic unit throughout the Phanerozoic or whether significant
M
16 rotations occurred in early Palaeozoic times between the Anabar- Angara and Aldan blocks is still a
17 matter of debate. Addressing this Dproblem a detailed palaeomagnetic study of sections of mid
18 Cambrian and Llandeillian ageE has been carried out along the river Lena, river Maya, river
19 Kulumbe, and river Stolbovaya, with a total of 403 collected hand-samples.
T
20 A section of Llandeilian Page was also investigated on the Russian Platform, near St. Petersburg.
21 The studied rocks are carbonates or fine grained terrigenous sediments of reddish and greyish
E
22 colors. Stepwise thermal demagnetization experiments reveal a rather simple directional behavior.
C
23 In most samples, after removal of a secondary magnetizations at low to intermediate temperatures,
C
24 a high temperature component is isolated, which is carried by magnetite and/or hematite.
A
25 Positive reversal tests and fold tests clearly demonstrate the primary character of the latter
26 component. While only reversed polarity directions are obtained in the lower two thirds of the
27 Llandeilo, six magnetozones of normal polarity are found in the Upper Llandeilo, which mark the
28 end of the Moyero reverse superchron.
29 Together with previously published paleomagnetic data our new results show rather systematic
30 difference in declinations of ~20° between the Aldan and Anabar-angara blocks. This argues in
31 favor of a relative rotation between these two blocks, with an Euler pole of rotation located at
32 latitude ~ 62ºN and Longitude ~ 117°. Our interpretation is further supported by existing results
33 from deep sounding seismic experiments, yielding a very similar pole of rotation.
34
35
36
37 Introduction

### page_3
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
2
38 The Siberian platform represents an important tectonic unit of the Earth crust and
39 understanding its geodynamic history is of great importance for deciphering the geological
40 evolution during the early Palaeozoic. Nevertheless, one of the key questions whether Siberia has
41 to be treated as a coherent structural unit since its amalgamation during the Palaeoproterozoic, or
T
42 whether independent units can be identified which have been subjected to subsequent relative
P
43 rotation and/or translation remains unanswered.
I
44 Based on differences in the geological and structuralR inventory, the Siberian platform can be
45 divided into three main tectonic elements (Fig.1). These are, the Anabar-Angara block, in the
C
46 southwestern, western and northern part of the platform, the Aldan block, in the southeastern part
S
47 and the v-shaped Vilyui syneclise separating Aldan from Anabar-Angara. The Vilyui syneclise
U
48 itself is filled with a thick sequence of Palaeozoic and Mesozoic deposits and covers the NE
N
49 trending Vilyui rift system of Middle Palaeozoic age.
A
50 Significant differences between palaeomagnetic pole positions for the Mid-Ordovician from
M
51 Anabar-Aldan (Moyero river valley) and Angara (Lena river valley) have been noted earlier[1]
52 and been interpreted as the consequen ce of post Middle Ordovician rotations between the two
D
53 areas. However, whether these rotations are local or can be traced on a regional scale has so far
E
54 not been unambiguously elaborated.
T
55 Subsequently, Pavlov and Gallet [2] carried out a detailed palaeomagnetic study of a
P
56 Cambrian-Ordovician section along the Moyero river and confirming the above observation they
E
57 indicated that systematic differences in palaeomagnetic pole positions with respect to the Apparent
C
58 Polar Wander Path (APWP) for southeastern Siberia [3] are present throughout the sections,
59 ranging from tChe Late Cambrian to the Early Silurian. Due to the variable quality of the
60 palaeomagnAetic data and uncertainties in temporal resolution of the different data sets, Pavlov and
61 Gallet [2] did not fully support the block rotation model, but pointed out that more data are needed
62 for Siberia before a final interpretation can be reached.
63 It has been shown earlier [4] that the discordant palaeomagnetic pole positions from nearly
64 coeval sections of Middle Riphean age from the northwest of the Siberian Platform (Turukhansk)
65 and the southeast (Uchur-Maya) can be matched if rotations between the southeastern part of the
66 Siberian Platform (Aldan Block) and the rest of platform are allowed. These rotations, likely to be
67 Mid Palaeozoic in age, can be related to the opening of the Vilyui rift about a rotation pole located
68 on the southwestern margin of the Vilyui syneclise, approximately at 117˚E longitude and 62˚N
69 latitude This interpretation was supported by Smethurst et al. [5], albeit with a slightly different
70 rotation pole at Long. 100˚E, Lat. 60˚N. It should be pointed out, however, that Smethurst et al.
71 [5], and, more recently, Cocks and Torsvik [6] point out relative rotations between the northern and
72 southern Siberian platform whereas in the model proposed by Pavlov and Petrov [4] rotations of

### page_4
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
3
73 the Aldan block relative to Anabar-Angara are the main issue. In addition, the comparison of
74 Middle to Late Cambrian palaeomagnetic poles from the northwest (Kulumbe river section),
75 northeast (Olenek river section) and south of the Siberian platform (Angara river region) did not
76 yield any significant differences between the palaeomagnetic data from these areas [7] therefore
T
77 rendering significant rotations within the Anabar-Angara block, as postulated in Smethurst et al [5]
P
78 as extremely unlikely. On the other hand, palaeomagnetic data for the Mid Ordovician from Aldan,
I
79 satisfying modern quality standards [8], support rotations beRtween Aldan and Anabar–Angara.
80 Unfortunately, however, only two high quality data sets from coeval rocks from Aldan and Anabar-
C
81 Angara are currently available and can be used to test the hypothesis described above. These are
S
82 the results for the Malgina (Aldan block) and Linok (Anabar-Angara block) formations both of
U
83 Middle Riphean age [2, 4, 7]and for rocks from the Moyero river section (Anabar-Angara block,
N
84 [2]) and the Polovinka section (Aldan block, [8]), both of Llandeilian age [9].
A
85 Despite the fact that the synchronicity of the Malgina and Linok formations seems to be
M
86 rather well established [10, 11], the contemporaneity was disputed and it was postulated that the
87 different pole positions for the two fo rmations can be explained by motions of the Siberian
D
88 platform in toto without the need to invoke relative displacements between the two blocks [12].
E
89 Llandeilian pole positions from the Moyero river section (Anabar block, [13]) and from the
T
90 Polovinka section (Aldan block, [8]) are difficult to be disputed as they meet modern quality
P
91 requirements and the sections studied clearly cover the same age intervals [9].
E
92 Here, we present new palaeomagnetic results for the Middle Cambrian of the Aldan block,
C
93 which will be compared to recently published results for rocks of the same age from the Anabar-
94 Angara block C [14, 15].
95 TheA first version of a regional Palaeozoic magnetic polarity time scale was published in a
96 monograph by Khramov et al. [16]. . This magnetostratigraphic time scale was further refined by
97 Khramov and Rodionov [17] and used, with minor modifications by Trench et al. [18] for the
98 construction of a global Ordovician magnetic polarity sequence. However, the Russian data
99 mentioned above are (a) based on very limited demagnetization experiments, (b) details of which
100 are unpublished, (c) published details are rarely sufficient to match the magnetostratigraphic data
101 to biostratigraphy and (d) almost all data used are from sediments from the Lena river valley.
102 Therefore, resampling of Ordovician key sections in Siberia is required in order to improve the
103 quality of the magnetostratigraphic database.
104 In two previous studies Pavlov et al. [8] and Gallet and Pavlov[13] published data for the
105 Llandeilo of the Moyero and Polovinka key sections.In this paper we present new data from three
106 additional sections of Llandeilian age from the Siberian platform. In addition, results from a
107 magnetostratigraphic investigation of a Llandeilian section, exposed in the Alexeevka quarry

### page_5
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
4
108 (Leningrad Oblast, northwestern East-European platform) will be presented which are used to
109 support the reliability of the Siberian data.
110 The magnetostratigraphy of the Ordovician of the East European platform was intensively
111 studied by Claesson [19], Trench et al. [18], Torsvik and Trench [20, 21]. These studies, however,
T
112 were limited to the limestones from South Sweden. The large area of Ordovician sedimentary rocks
P
113 in the northwestern part of Russia was practically not studied with the noteworthy exception of the
I
114 Arenig to Lower Llanvirnian sections of the Lava and TosnRa rivers [5].
115
C
116
S
117 Geology and Stratigraphy
U
118
N
119 Middle Cambrian.
A
120 The Middle Cambrian deposits, studied here, are located in the Uchur-Maya region in the
M
121 South-East of the Siberian platform (Fig. 2) and excluding the uppermost part of the Inican
122 formations,. can be divided into the C haya and Ust’-Maya formations. The Chaya formation
D
123 reaches 60 m in thickness and is dominated by limestones, argillaceous limestones and marls of
E
124 reddish, greenish and grey colour. This formation is exposed in two massif cliffs along the right
T
125 bank of the Maya river (Supplementary file 8 in the Appendix for locations). Both cliffs were
P
126 sampled for this study and will be referred to as outcrop A, where 50 and outcrop B, were 30
E
127 oriented hand samples were collected, respectively.
C
128 The Ust’-Maya formation, mostly greenish and grey-greenish limestones and clayish
129 limestones is eCxposed in a series of outcrops of reduced thickness, predominantly along the left
130 bank of theA lower Maya river. The stratigraphic thickness of the Ust’-Maya formation, exposed
131 along the Maya river valley totals up to about 500m. Nine outcrops of the Ust’-Maya formation
132 were sampled and 113 oriented hand samples were taken.
133 Both, the Chaya and Ust’-Maya formations contain rich faunal assemblages of trilobites and
134 acritarchs which define their biostratigraphic positions [22]. The Chaya formation corresponds to
135 the trilobite index zones Tomagnostus fissus/Paradoxides sacheri (uppermost part of Amgian
136 stage) and Corynexochus perforatus/Anopolenus henrici (lowermost part of Mayan stage). The
137 Ust’Maya formation correlates with two upper trilobite index zones of Mayan stage –
138 Anomocariodes limbataeformis and Lejopyge laevigata/Aldanaspis truncata.
139 All studied Middle Cambrian rocks are practically flat lying and maximum tilt does not
140 exceed 3°.
141
142 Llandeilo.

### page_6
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
5
143 Based on recently published biostratigraphic time scales [23], the Llandeilo is interpreted to
144 be the upper part of the Llanvirn and to correspond to graptolite zone Glyptograptus teretiusculus.
145 The Ordovician of the Siberian platform is divided into 14 regional stages (horizons) three of
146 which (from bottom to top the Volgian, Kirensky and Kudrian) are correlated with the
T
147 G.teretiusculus zone [9] and, thus, correspond to the Llandeilo of the Fortey et al. [23] standard
P
148 scale. Whereas both the Kirensky and Kudrinsky horizons can be definitely traced into the
I
149 Ordovician of the Lena river, their stratigraphic differentiatRion is more difficult elsewhere on the
150 platform and consequently, the Kirenskian and Kudrian beds are often grouped into the
C
151 undifferentiated Kirinsko-Kudrian horizon.
S
152 During the field seasons of 1998-2001 three sedimentary sections of Llandeilian age from
U
153 the NW, W and SSE of the Siberian platform were studied in detail.
N
154 The Kulumbe section (Fig.1, and Table 1) is situated along the Kulumbe river valley,
A
155 downstream the “Silurian” rapids. Here, rocks of Llandeilian age (Kirensko-Kudrian horizon),
M
156 composed of red and greenish-grey siltstones and mudstones with intercalation of grey marls, were
157 sampled on the left bank of the river immediately below the Zagorninsky sill of Permian-Triassic
D
158 age. Early Carboniferous deformation [24, 25] resulted in tilting between 15° to 25°.
E
159 In total, 35 hand samples were taken from the lower and middle parts of the Kirensko-
T
160 Kudrian horizon with a sampling spacing between 0.2 and 1 m.
P
161 The second section is exposed on the left bank of river Stolbovaya, 6 km up-stream from its
E
162 mouth. This section includes a continuous stratigraphic record spanning from Llandeilo (Volginsky
C
163 horizon) to Lower Ashgill. It contains rich fossil assemblages [26] and is mainly composed by
164 grey, greenish C–grey limestones and marls with the exception of the red coloured Kirensko-
165 Kudrinsky hAorizon, where more than 50 hand samples were taken in sampling intervals of 0.3 to
166 0.6m.
167 A third section studied is located in the upper valley of the Lena river near the village of
168 Kudrino (Fig.1) and represents one of the most important Ordovician key sections on the Siberian
169 platform [9]. The lower part of the section (Kirensky horizon) is represented by grey aleuritic
170 sandstones and greenish mudstones, overlain by the Kudrinsky horizon, mostly brown and greyish
171 brown aleuritic sandstones interbedded with greenish mudstones. The top of the section
172 corresponds to the Chertovsky horizon (Caradoc) and consist of greenish-gray mudstones in the
173 lower part and of red beds (mudstones and siltstones) in the upper part. 125 block samples were
174 taken in the Kudrino section with a vertical sample spacing of 0.1-0.5 m.
175 The additionally studied European section is situated in the Leningrad oblast in a quarry
176 near Alexeevka, Kingisp district, and represents almost the complete Llandeilo with the exception
177 of the lowermost beds. The lower 3 m of the Alexeevka section belong to the Mednikova group of

### page_7
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
6
178 the Uhaku stage and are composed of bluish grey limestones and argillaceous limestones. The next
179 6m above correspond to the Viivikonna formation of the Kukruse stage and are made up by dark
180 limestones, sometimes argillaceous and bituminous, with intercalations of kukersites (oil shales,
181 rich in algae). Both the Mednikovo and Vivikonna formations are rich in benthic fauna and in
T
182 microfossils [27]. In total, about 140 hand samples were taken here with sampling intervals of
P
183 0.05-0.1 m.
I
184 R
185
C
186 Laboratory Procedures
S
187
U
188 Oriented hand samples were cut into cubes of 8 cm3 and directions and intensities of the
N
189 Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) were measured using a vertically oriented 2G three axis
A
190 cryogenic magnetometer in the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Department for Earth and
M
191 Environmental Sciences, Ludwig-Maximilians-University, Munich and in the Palaeomagnetic
192 Laboratory of the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris. All samples were subjected to stepwise
D
193 thermal demagnetization experiments, reaching maximum temperatures of up to 680°C. Mineral
E
194 alteration during heating was monitored by measurements of low field susceptibility with a mini-
T
195 kappa susceptibility bridge. The magnetometers, as well as the furnaces used for thermal
P
196 demagnetization (Schoenstedt, TSD-1 in Munich and laboratory-built oven in Paris) experiments,
E
197 are housed in magnetically shielded rooms. The demagnetization results were analyzed using
C
198 orthogonal vector plots [28] and stereographic projections. Linear and planar elements in the
199 demagnetizatioCn data were identified by eye and subjected to principal component analysis [29].
200 A
201 Palaeomagnetic Results
202
203 Maya River Section (Middle Cambrian)
204 Chaya formation
205 Thermal demagnetization experiments reveal the presence of two magnetic components
206 (Supplementary file 1 in the Appendix) in almost all samples from the Chaya formation. A low-
207 temperature component (LT) is isolated at demagnetization temperatures of up to 350-400ºC and
208 has a direction very close to the direction of the present day Earth’s magnetic field at the site. A
209 high-temperature component (HT), carried by hematite, is observed above 400–450ºC and up to
210 680ºC. The HT component is of dual polarity, with south-southwest (north-northeast) declinations
211 and upward (downward) moderate inclinations (Fig. 3a).

### page_8
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
7
212 A relatively large overlap between the LT and HT components often occurs in the
213 intermediate to high-temperature range. Consequently, the HT component directions are sometimes
214 biased by the LT component and cannot be determined by principal-component analysis
215 (Supplementary file 1 in the Appendix, sample 3). Attempts using alternative field (AF)
T
216 demagnetization to enhance the identification of components, failed. Finally, chemical alteration
P
217 above 450°C and the formation of new magnetic phases often disguises the “true” direction of the
I
218 HT component. Nevertheless, despite these difficulties we hRave managed to determine the direction
219 of the HT component in the majority of the samples (Supplementary file 8 in the Appendix); mean
C
220 directions calculated for normal and reversed directions [30] pass the reversal test with
S
221 classification C [31]. This suggests that the resulting overall mean for the Chaya section is a rather
U
222 reliable estimate of the magnetic field of time of acquisition of the HT.
N
223
A
224 Ust’-Maya formation
M
225 Generally, the magnetization of rocks of the Ust’-Maya formation is two to three times
226 weaker, than the magnetization of roc ks from the Chaya formation (Supplementary file 2 in the
D
227 Appendix). The magnetization of the majority of the samples contains either solely one component
E
228 of recent origin, removed at 300-400ºC, or is a composition of LT and HT components. The
T
229 presence of HT is well defined by great circle tracks when plotted in stereographic projection.
P
230 Rather weak magnetization in combination with chemical alteration above 440-460ºC, prevents
E
231 the direct identification of HT in these samples.
C
232 Nevertheless, among the more than 100 samples from the Ust’-Maya formation studied,
233 there are 24 wiCth demagnetization properties allowing the identification of “end-point” directions
234 for the HT cAomponent (Supplementary file 8 in the Appendix). Judging by the maximum
235 unblocking temperatures observed (Supplementary file 2 in the Appendix) this component is
236 mainly carried by magnetite. The majority of the “useable” samples originates from the lower part
237 of the Ust’-Maya formation. It is interesting to note that there are examples indicating that in
238 addition to LT, some samples can contain two, probably antipodal ancient components (see
239 Supplementary file 2 in the Appendix, sample 123). This might indicate that occasionally the
240 acquisition of magnetization spanned a prolonged time interval. Like the HT component
241 identified in samples from the Chaya formation, the HT component, isolated in the Ust’-Maya
242 formation is of dual polarity (Fig.3b) but does not pass the reversal test. This might be explained by
243 some degree of contamination by a LT component.
244 The mean directions of the Chaya and Ust’-Maya formations are very close to each other,
245 which can be expected on the basis of data published earlier for rocks of the Amgian and Mayan
246 stage [14]. This also implies that averaging directions of normal and reversed polarities into a

### page_9
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
8
247 common mean reduces the influence of LT contamination significantly. This is in accord with the
248 positive reversal test when all the HT directions from both the Chaya and Ust’-Maya formations
249 are grouped together (Supplementary file 8 in the Appendix).
250 From the data presented here, it becomes evident that the Middle Cambrian section of the
T
251 Maya river valley contains numerous intervals of normal and reversed polarity (Fig.2), which is
P
252 compatible with magnetostratigraphic data obtained from north Siberian key sections of the
I
253 Amgian and Mayan stage [14, 32]. This fact as well as the pRositive reversal test, the lack of
254 resemblance to palaeomagnetic directions of younger age and the independence of the HT
C
255 component from the magnetic mineralogy allow us to tie the acquisition of magnetization closely
S
256 to the time of deposition of the rocks studied.
U
257
N
258 Kulumbe section (Llandeilo)
A
259 After removal of unstable magnetizations at low demagnetization temperatures, only one
M
260 stable component of magnetization which is characterized by rather steep inclinations, can be
261 identified in some part of samples, (S upplementary file 3 in the Appendix, sample 638-TC). The
D
262 direction of this component is very close to the direction of the characteristic components identified
E
263 in the Zagorninsky sill (Fig. 3c) [33], suggesting a Permian-Triassic age of remagnetization.
T
264 In addition, some samples show the presence of only one stable component with
P
265 northwestern declinations and shallow to moderately positive inclinations. Usually, however, the
E
266 magnetization of the samples studied is controlled by the combination of the components described
C
267 above. Whereas the trap related remagnetization component is removed usually in the temperature
268 interval 270-60C0˚C, the second component is more stable and shows maximum unblocking
269 temperatureAs near the Curie point of hematite. The mean direction of this component
270 (Supplementary file 9 in the Appendix) is close to mean directions obtained earlier for Llanvirnian
271 rocks of the Kulumbe section [15] and coincides practically with the mean direction of Llandeilian
272 rocks from the Moyero river[13], recalculated to the coordinates of the Kulumbe section (Fig. 3d).
273 It should be noted, that the ChRM‘s from the various sections approach significantly after
274 correction for local tilts, thus yielding a positive regional fold test and pointing towards a pre-
275 Carboniferous age of magnetization.
276
277 Stolbovaya section (Llandeilo)
278 The magnetization of the sedimentary rocks of the Stolbovaya section is strongly affected
279 by the trap intrusions [34]. Nevertheless, a considerable part of the redbeds within the Kirensky-
280 Kudrian horizon preserved traces of an ancient magnetization. The various types of behaviour of
281 the samples during thermal demagnetization are shown in Supplementary file 4 in the Appendix.

### page_10
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
9
282 While sample ST-233 is completely remagnetized, there are examples for successful isolation of a
283 characteristic HT magnetization with northwesterly declinations and shallow inclination (sample
284 ST-220 in Supplementary file 4 in the Appendix). However, the essential part of the studied
285 collection is marked by a very strong overlap of the “trap magnetization” and, what is believed to
T
286 be, an ancient component (Supplementary file 4 in the Appendix, samples ST-203, ST-206, ST-
P
287 216).
I
288 However, this directional overlap does not preclude Rthe determination of the polarity of the
289 ancient component when regarding the trend of remagnetization circles. The combination of great
C
290 circles and endpoint data [35] yields a mean direction for the Stolbovaya section (Fig.3,
S
291 Supplementary file 9 in the Appendix) which is very close to the expected direction for the
U
292 Llandeilo (based on the data from the Moyero and Kulumbe sections). This result indicates that the
N
293 characteristic HT component was acquired during deposition or briefly after it.
A
294
M
295 Kudrino section (Llandeilo)
296 After removal of an unstable m agnetization below 300°C, almost all samples from the
D
297 Kudrino section show the presence of the dual polarity HT component together with an middle
E
298 temperature component (MT) of normal polarity (fig. 4a,c,e). Whereas the HT component decays
T
299 towards the origin of the orthogonal diagram, MT component practically always is intermediate
P
300 (Supplementary file 6 in the Appendix, samples 24c-TC, 60-TC).
E
301 Maximum unblocking temperatures of both components are usually well above 600˚C,
C
302 clearly indicating hematite as the principal carrier of the stable magnetization. The similarity in
303 blocking tempeCrature range does not facilitate distinction between both components, however the
304 clear differeAnce of their directions (Fig. 4f) as well as the comparison with stratigraphically
305 adjacent samples allow to solve positively this question.
306 The mean direction for the intermediate (MT) component (Fig 4d,e, Supplementary file 9 in
307 the Appendix) has about the same direction as the corresponding MT mean (Fig. 4 d,e,f) of the
308 Mid Ordovician Polovinka section (middle valley of the Lena river), considered as being Late
309 Ordovician or Early Silurian in age [8]. Therefore we suggest that the former is also of secondary
310 origin.
311 The HT component isolated in rocks of the Chertovskian and the Kudrian horizons is of
312 dual polarity and close to passing the reversal test (γ/γ = 15.0°/10.2° and 13.2°/10.3°
c
313 correspondingly).
314 The comparison of the distributions of the HT vectors of reversed polarity of the Polovinka
315 and Kudrino sections yields differences in mean declination in the order of 15-20° (Fig.4a,b,f).
316 This is compatible with block rotation models proposed earlier [7] on the base of data for Middle-

### page_11
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
10
317 Late Cambrian rocks from the Lena river. All this allows us to interpret the HT component,
318 isolated in the Kudrian and Chertovskian horizon to be of pre-rotational origin and having been
319 acquired during deposition or soon after. No directions of the ChRM with normal polarity have
320 been identified in the lower (Kirensky) part of the Kudrino section [see also 36].
T
321
P
322 Alexeevka section (Llandeilo)
I
323 Examples of demagnetization diagrams are represenRted in Supplementary file 6 in the
324 Appendix. All samples from the Alexeevka quarry are rather weakly magnetized. Nevertheless,
C
325 based on the intensity of magnetization and demagnetization behavior, the collection can be
S
326 divided into two groups (Fig.3f).
U
327 The first group includes samples with magnetizations in the order of 3-6 .10-5 A/m carrying
N
328 either one or two components of magnetization. Single component samples are demagnetized
A
329 between 250 and 300˚C and yield directions scattered around the direction of the modern field. If
M
330 two components of magnetization are present, heating above 200°C reveals a directional
331 component pointing to the south-sout heast with rather steep positive inclinations. Maximum
D
332 unblocking temperatures reach 400°C before the intensity of magnetization either drops below the
E
333 sensitivity of the magnetometer or the directions are obscured by chemical alteration. AF –
T
334 demagnetization experiments after initial heating up to 190° to 250°C reveal maximum
P
335 coercitivities of the characteristic component of magnetization of about 10 to 50 nT, indicating
E
336 magnetite as principal carrier of magnetization.
C
337 The resulting mean direction (Supplementary file 9 in the Appendix) is in excellent
338 agreement withC the expected direction for the Llandeilo (Fig.3g), calculated from the 463 Ma poles
339 of the APWAP for Baltica [5]. This supports our interpretation that this magnetization is indeed of
340 Llandeilian age. The second group includes only a small number of samples; however these
341 samples show a much stronger magnetization and behave more stable during demagnetization
342 (Supplementary file 6 in the Appendix ). The resulting directions of the ChRM strongly resembles
343 directions associated with Mesozoic age remagnetizations which are typical for this region [5]. We
344 therefore interpret the magnetizations observed in these samples to reflect a Mesozoic
345 remagnetization event.
346
347 Magnetostratigraphy
348 The magnetostratigraphy of the sections studied is shown in Figures 5 and 6. Quite often
349 stable end point directions could successfully be identified. Nevertheless, there are many samples,
350 where this was prevented by either overlapping unblocking spectra or chemical alteration during

### page_12
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
11
351 thermal demagnetization. In the majority of these cases, however, it was possible to unequivocally
352 establish the magnetic polarity based on the trend of remagnetization circles.
353 The most notable feature of all magnetostratigraphic records, obtained here, is the
354 predominance of directions of reversed polarity. So far, no primary directions of normal polarity
T
355 have been identified in the lower two thirds of the Llandeilo on the Siberian platform. Isolated
P
356 samples from the Volginsky and the Kirensky horizons of the Polovinka section, carrying normal
I
357 polarities have been considered to reflect Mid Palaeozoic reRmagnetizations [8].
358 The same reasoning can be applied to two zones of normal polarity isolated in the
C
359 Volginsky horizon of the Kudrino section by Rodionov et al. [36] with mean directions very close
S
360 to the ones of much younger sediments from the middle Lena river [37]. There are also no
U
361 indications for the existence of a normal polarity zone in the Alexeevka quarry (Baltica) with
N
362 exception of the uppermost levels. However, Torsvik and Trench [20, 21] found one sample with a
A
363 normal polarity direction in the middle of the Llandeilo in the Hallekis section and some samples
M
364 of normal polarity directions from two stratigraphic levels of the Gullhogen quarry, South Sweden
365 also of Mid Llandeilian age. Hence, f ollowing Trench et al. [18] we include this zone in the
D
366 composite magnetostratigraphic sequence of the Llandeilo. In agreement with Torsvik and Trench
E
367 [21] we note, however, that at least the part of the data supporting the existence of this normal
T
368 polarity zone, is only of moderate quality and more detailed sampling is required in the future in
P
369 order to confirm this polarity zone.
E
370 The magnetostratigraphic record from the Llandeilo of the Kudrino section yields clear
C
371 indication for the presence of at least three zones of normal polarity. The presence of several
372 normal polarityC zones in the upper part of the Llandeilo is also supported by the data from the
373 Moyero, PoAlovinka and Alexeevka sections. Irrespectively whether three or more zones of normal
374 polarity are present in the Llandeilian age sections studied so far, it is obvious that termination of
375 the Llandeilo coincides with the termination of a long reversed polarity interval referred to as
376 Moyero superchron by Pavlov and Gallet [38] which lasted ~20-30 Myr.
377 Furthermore, in the Kudrino section, a short period of normal polarity can be observed just
378 above the Llandeilo-Caradoc transition. This short period of normal polarity is followed again by a
379 short interval of reversed polarity before the onset of a rather long lasting interval of normal
380 polarity. This pattern, two rather short intervals of normal and inverse polarity followed by a long
381 interval of normal polarity is compatible with data from the Gullhogen quarry, South Sweden[21]
382
383 Palaeomagnetic data and the relative rotation between the Aldan and Anabar-Angara blocks.
384 Based on the magnetostratigraphy established results obtained in this study we can now
385 compare palaeomagnetic data, which are exactly coeval and which have been obtained by applying

### page_13
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
12
386 modern laboratory and analytical techniques. In Fig.7a the Llandeilian palaeopoles of the Kulumbe,
387 Moyero, Stolbovaya, Polovinka and Kudrino sections are presented as well as the palaeomagnetic
388 pole, obtained by Torsvik et al. [37] for the Llandeilo of the mid stream Lena river valley.
389 Paleopoles from the Anabar-Angara block (Siberian platform to the west of the axis of the Vilyui
T
390 syneclise) form a tight group and are distinctly different from the poles derived from sections
P
391 located in the south-eastern (Aldanian) part of the Siberian platform.
I
392 The Kudrino section, which is situated near the axis Rof the Vilyui syneclise yields an
393 intermediate pole position. All the palaeomagnetic poles are close to or lie on a small circle
C
394 centered about a pole of rotation located near the northern shore of lake Baikal. This location is
S
395 very close to the Euler pole proposed earlier by Pavlov and Petrov [4] and used to match the
U
396 palaeomagnetic poles of coeval Riphean formations from NW and SE of the Siberian platform. In
N
397 addition, it is important to note that Mid-Riphean poles from Turukhansk and Uchur-Maya regions
A
398 not only lie on small circles centered on the same pole of rotation (Fig.7a), but also the angle
M
399 between the palaeomagnetic pole positions for the Llandeilo is comparable to the one for the
400 Riphean poles (20–25°).
D
401 The Middle Cambrian paleomagnetic pole obtained in this study is a new strong argument
E
402 for the existence of a significant angular difference between paleomagnetic data sets of the Anabar-
T
403 Angara and Aldan blocks. This pole in combination with coeval and nearly coeval ones from the
P
404 Angara –Anabar block defines a small circle segment covering 20° which is centered on the same
E
405 pole of rotation as discussed above (fig.7a,b).
C
406 These observations agree very well with older palaeomagnetic data sets of considerably
407 lower quality. C
408 DurAing the 60s and 70s many palaeomagnetic directions have been obtained for the rocks of
409 the Upper Cambrian Verkholensk formation from outcrops along the valley of river Lena and along
410 the upper stream of the Angara river. Despite the fact that these results do not meet modern quality
411 criteria, we believe that they provide relatively reliable pole positions and can lend additional
412 support to our interpretations. With the exception of the polarity transition zones, the NRM of these
413 rocks is mainly carried by one component with minor overprinting by a very steep secondary
414 component of recent origin [39]. The latter can considerably affect the inclination of the resulting
415 total vector, with minor effects on the declination. We also note that the results for the Verkholensk
416 formation were obtained by averaging of numerous directions of normal and reversed polarity
417 which strongly reduces the bias due to overprints.
418 Plotting the distribution of declinations from the Verkholensk formation as a function of
419 geographic position reveals that the variability in declination reflects clockwise rotation when
420 moving from southwest to northeast (Fig. 7c). This is also true for the longitudes of the

### page_14
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
13
421 palaeomagnetic pole positions which are clearly controlled by the geographic location of the
422 sampling sites (Fig. 7d). The corresponding pole positions are shown in Figure 7b. In concordance
423 with the results for the Llandeilian, Middle Cambrian and Riphean, the distribution of pole position
424 also describes a small circle centered around a common Euler pole.
T
425 In addition to the pole positions from the Verkholensk formation, recently published poles
P
426 for the Upper and Middle Cambrian deposits of the Moyero, Kulumbe, Khorbusuonka and Olenek
I
427 rivers sections [13-15, 40] are also shown in Fig.7b. We notRe that the rather tight cluster of all
428 middle to upper Cambrian poles from the Angara-Anabar block, clearly indicates its crustal
C
429 coherence since at least the Middle Cambrian. This observation is not compatible with the Euler
S
430 pole positions suggested by Smethurst et al. [5].
U
431
N
432 Determination of the Euler Pole for the Aldan and Anabar-Angara blocks
A
433
M
434 In a first step, the data set (see Table 1) is divided into four subsets according to the
435 stratigraphic ages: mid Riphean (two poles), Middle Cambrian (4 poles), Late Cambrian (17 poles)
D
436 and Llandeilian (6 poles). In a second step, the surface of the globe is covered by a grid of evenly
E
437 spaced points (for example 1 x 1°) and for each grid point as for centre of a circle the optimum
T
438 small circle for each of the 4 subsets is calculated. As a measure of the quality of the fit, the
P
439 residuals, which are the sum of squares of angular distances between the individual
E
440 palaeomagnetic poles and the corresponding small circles, have been calculated for each grid point.
C
441 The total residual value, calculated for each grid point, is considered as the estimate for the location
442 of the Euler poCle at a given grid point. Regions on the globe containing the grid points with the
443 smallest resAiduals, are considered to be the most likely area where the location of the Euler pole is
444 to be expected.
445 The distribution of calculated residual values on the Earth surface is shown in
446 Supplementary file 7 in the Appendix. The area with the smallest residuals is centered at 54.5º N
447 and 111.5º E, which, taking into account the accuracy of available palaeomagnetic data, is in quite
448 good agreement with the Euler pole, proposed earlier by Pavlov and Petrov [41].
449
450 Geometry of the Vilyui basin’s earth crust and the relative rotation of Aldan and Anabar-
451 Angara blocks.
452 The hypothesis that the Aldan-Anabar block rotations are linked to the opening of the
453 Vilyui rift system, was discussed and challenged by McElhinny and McFadden [42] and
454 Pisarevsky and Natapov [12]. The main point raised by these authors is that such rotations should

### page_15
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
14
455 have induced a break up of the Siberian craton. This motivated us to look more closer at the
456 geometry of the crustal basement of the Vilyui syneclise.
457 During the 1970s and 80s Siberian platform has been studied by long range refraction
458 seismic experiments. Three of these seismic lines (CRATON, KIMBERLITE, BATHOLITE)
T
459 crossed the Vilyui basin (Fig.1). Interpreted crustal cross-sections for the two first profiles [43, 44]
P
460 are presented in Fig. 8. The geometry of the crustal boundaries allows us to estimate the amount of
I
461 extension during the formation the Vilyui depression. R
462 Continuous decrease, observed in the width of the Vilyui basin and in sedimentary
C
463 thickness along its SW to NE axis suggests that the basin was opened in a scissors-like mode.
S
464 Therefore, the amount of horizontal extension in different cross-sections may provide information
U
465 on the position of the pole of opening.
N
466 In extensional basins, the thickness of the crust is controlled by external forces due to
A
467 deformational changes in rock volume and in temperature. The changes in rock volume are small
M
468 and neglected in most models. On the other hand, the temperature of the lithosphere increases
469 during extension and then decreases a fterward back to the steady state [45]. Assuming that the
D
470 extension in the Vilyui basin occurred during the Palaeozoic [46] and that the 40 km-thick crust
E
471 returns to the steady state temperature after about 55 my [45], we can consider that the temperature
T
472 profile before extension was close to the present day one, and the thermal effect is negligible. Thus,
P
473 we conclude that the difference between the basin axes crustal thickness prior to extension
E
474 (referred to as H (x)) and after (referred to as H (x)) is mostly caused by deformation. Using the
0 1
C
475 principle of mass conservation, we can pose the following equation:
476 C
A L 1 L
477 ∫H (x)dx =∫H (x)dx (1)
1 0
0 0
478 where L and L1 are respectively the length of the deformed area before and after extension.
479
480 The seismic profiles provide data on the present-day crustal thickness, while to estimating the
481 crustal geometry before extension requires some assessments. Assuming that crustal thickness
482 before extension changed linearly between the present-day thickness of the undeformed internal
483 parts of the Anabar and Aldan blocks, the formula (1) then gives an estimate of the length of the
484 extended area before deformation:
L
1
485 L= ∫H (x)dx/H (2)
1 av
0
486
487 where H is the average value of the Aldan and Anabar crustal thickness.
av

### page_16
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
15
488 To estimate the amount of stretching along the seismic profiles it is necessary to estimate
489 the present-day limits of the extended area. The thickness of the Earth crust at the end points of the
490 chosen interval estimates the pre-extensional crustal thickness. Seismic data provide the depth to
491 the crystalline basement and to the Moho. Crustal thickness within the basin is then derived by the
T
492 difference between these values.
P
493 Possible sources of error are: incorrect seismic estimates of crustal thickness, variations of
I
494 crustal thickness in the area of the Vilyui basin before extenRsion and an erroneous choice in the
495 limits of the extended area. An error analysis, however, shows that formula (2) is very robust
C
496 (Supplementary file 11 in the Appendix).
S
497 Let us now estimate the amount of extension for two profiles crossing the Vilyui basin. For
U
498 the profile CRATON, the thicknesses of the Anabar and Aldan crust are estimated to be 44 and 42
N
499 km, respectively, the width of the extended area to be 920 km, which gives an extension of ~234
A
500 km (~30%). This estimate can be compared to the McKenzie extension model [45]. Along this
M
501 profile, the crustal thickness is ~20 km in the deepest part of the basin; the extension ratio is thus
502 β=(44+42)/(2*20)=2.15. Accord ing to [45], this would produces ~8.6 km of synextensional
D
503 subsidence and ~4.7 km of thermal post-extensional subsidence. This corresponds well to the
E
504 seismic data when suggesting densities of 3.2, 2.9 and 2.4 103kg/m3 for the mantle, the crust and
*
T
505 the sediments, respectively.
P
506 The profile KIMBERLITE provides a smaller estimate of extension, ~45km for a present-
E
507 day length ~662 km for the stretched area. This gives an average extension of ~7%. (The thickness
C
508 is here ~38.7 km for the crust of Anabar and ~ 43.6 km for the crust of Aldan). The minimal crustal
509 thickness alongC KIMBERLITE is 26.6 km, hence the maximum extensional ratio is equal to 1.55,
510 which accoArding to [45] yields a value of 5.5 km for the synextensional subsidence and of 3.1 km
511 for the thermal subsidence. This values again appear in good agreement with the seismic data.
512 From the estimates above, one can find that the pole of basin opening was situated at a
513 distance ~ 93 km to the south-west of profile KIMBERLITE (Fig. 9). We tested the robustness of
514 these values by changing the parameters used in the model. In any cases, the distance does not
515 exceed 100 km (Supplementary file 10 in the Appendix).
516
517 Discussion
518 If the determination of the position of the centre of opening of the Vilyui basin is correct, it
519 would be manifested by compressional tectonics to the south-west from this location. Indeed, the
520 actual interpretation of seismic data obtained for profile BATHOLITE indicates an elevated
521 basement and crustal thickening, where the profile crosses the continuation of the Vilyui basin axis
522 (A..Egorkin – personal communication). Post- Early Silurian SW-NE oriented folds are known in

### page_17
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
16
523 the southern part of the Siberian platform adjacent to north-northwestern areas of the Baikal –
524 Patom fold-thrust belt (see Fig. 9). Recent data of industrial drill holes and seismic surveys in the
525 region of the Nepsk-Botuobinsk antyclise (Fig. 9) indicate that the thrust and fold-nappes are
526 widespread in this part of the Palaeozoic cover of the Siberian platform [47].
T
527 On the other hand the fan-like dyke swarms, rimming the Vilyui syneclise from NW and SE
P
528 are evidence for the extensional formation of the Vilyui basin to the northeast from the suggested
I
529 pole of opening. In the Middle of the 60s Shtekh [48] suggeRsted the existence of buried oceanic
530 crust under the northeastern margin of the Vilyui syneclise. Recent interpretation of seismic data
C
531 [44] supports this conclusion which is compatible with the hypothesis of Aldan – Anabar-Angara
S
532 blocks rotation.
U
533 The extensional pole lies within an area, where, according to palaeomagnetic data, the
N
534 location of Euler pole is rather probable (Fig. 9). The boundary of this area corresponds to a value
A
535 of the residual of R=1.6Ro, where Ro is the minimal value of the residual. Taking into account the
M
536 accuracy of the palaeomagnetic data, the compatibility is rather high. It is important that the angle
537 of opening of the basin based on exte nsional data is about the same as predicted from
D
538 palaeomagnetism. The rotation pole derived from extensional data ( Lat ≈62ºN; Long≈117ºE)
E
539 seems to be rather robust as it satisfies both geological and palaeomagnetic data.
T
540
P
541 Conclusion
E
542 Our new magnetostratigraphic results combined with published data allow to propose a
C
543 magnetic polarity sequence for Llandeilian times, which is characterized by the predominance of
544 reversed polariCty in its early part and by alternation of intervals of normal and reversed polarity (6
545 at least) in iAts later part.
546 The comparison of palaeomagnetic poles from the Aldan and Anabar-Angara blocks of the
547 Siberian platform obtained for four age levels (Middle Riphean, Middle Cambrian, Late Cambrian
548 and Middle Ordovician) demonstrates significant angular differences in declination.
549 This difference may be explained by relative rotation in the order of 20-25º of the Aldan
550 and Anabar-Angara blocks in post-Ordovician time about an Euler pole located somewhere to the
551 north-east from the northern shore of lake Baikal. Such a rotation requires imperatively the
552 extension of the Earth crust under the Vilyui basin, with increasing amounts from south-west to
553 north-east.
554 Extension rates along two crustal cross sections, based on results from long-range seismic
555 profiles, are compatible with the palaeomagnetic data and allow the definition of a rotation pole at:
556 Lat ≈62ºN; Long≈117ºE.
557

922 Supplementary material.
923 Analysis of stability of estimates of total extension using formula (2).
924
925 Possible sources of error in total extension estimates are: incorrect seismic estimates of
T
926 crustal thickness, variations of crustal thickness in the area of the Vilyui basin before extension and
P
927 erroneous choice of limits of the extended area. As formula (2) uses the integral of the crustal
I
928 thickness it is robust to local (short-term) variations of the cRrustal thickness. Significantly more
929 important, however, are systematic errors in estimates of the depth of the Moho. Suppose that the
C
930 depth determination for the Moho is wrong by a value of ΔH , then the estimate of the initial
S
931 crustal thickness will be wrong by the the same value, and the error in the estimate of the value L
U
932 will be in order of (ΔH H)2L. If the depth of the Moho is misidentified by 5 km, when the true
N
933 depth is about 45 km, then the error associated with the estimate of L will be about 1%. Suppose
A
934 that when applying formula (2) the left boundary of the extended area is shifted by values of δL
1
M
935 and the right was shifted by δL compared to the real limits of the extended area. Substituting into
2
936 formula (2) shows that the error inD the estimate of the amount of stretching ΔL = L −L will be
1
937 equal to (δL −δL)*δH /(2H E), where δH is the difference in crustal thickness at the left and the

942 AnotheCr possible source of error are changes in crustal thickness during the process of
943 extension cAaused by intrusion of magmatic rocks. These changes should be proportional to the
944 amount of extension. To estimate the position of the pole of opening we use the extensional ratio
945 along different profiles. It is easy to demonstrate that errors proportional to the extension do not
946 shift the location of the pole of rotation. Thus, we conclude that estimate (2) is very robust to
947 different sources of errors.
